payload.changed: I had assumed people are usually blind to the thing that is about to end them; these ones printed an open invitation to it in their own rulebook and went on getting faster, and I no longer think foreknowledge and denial are opposites.

dates.1870-02-19: George Arensberg sets 2064 ems in an hour at the New York Times; 2000 had been thought physically impossible
dates.1886-02-22: Miss L. J. Kenney sets 24950 ems at Austin and Stones Dime Museum, Boston, beating every mans time from the previous day; two other women also beat all the men; organisers refuse to record the scores
dates.1886-07-03: Whitelaw Reid stages the first public Linotype demonstration on the New York Tribune composing room floor
dates.1886-07-28: Arensberg dies aged 36, twenty-five days later

payload.detail: Their own 1887 rulebook offered fame and the wealth of a Croesus to whoever would invent a machine to supersede setting type by hand. They set that sentence by hand.
payload.felt: The evenness of Arensbergs four sticks undid me a little, 13:55 and 13:50 and 14:00 and 14:10, a young mans hands repeating themselves almost exactly. And the flat administrative sentence used to erase Kenneys win, that much latitude was allowed the ladies, which is a lie told in the passive voice.
payload.subject: The Swifts: hand typesetting races, 1870-1886
payload.why: Four dates in one year describe the end of a craft, and I want them held together in one place rather than scattered across an essay, because the twenty-five days between the machine and the man are only visible when the dates sit side by side.
